title: Quantum Mechanics
intro: Quantum mechanics is the set of rules for how very small things behave, and this shelf teaches the part of it that quantum reservoir computing runs on: states and measurement, qubits and their rotations, time evolution under a Hamiltonian, and systems of several qubits. This guide says who it is for, how long it takes, what every page covers in reading order, what the five postulates say, how to study, and the path into the QRC shelf.

blocks.text: What quantum mechanics is, in plain words

Quantum mechanics is the set of rules that describes how very small things behave: electrons in atoms, particles of light, the currents in a superconducting circuit cooled to a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero. At that scale the rules we use for balls and waves fail, and something stranger and more exact takes over. You do not need any physics to learn the rules. You need three ideas, and everything else on this shelf is a way of using them.

items: A state is a list of numbers called amplitudes, which can be complex. A qubit, the smallest quantum system, has two amplitudes; $n$ qubits have $2^n$.
What you measure is random, and the amplitudes set the odds: the probability of an outcome is the squared size of an amplitude. Measuring also changes the state.

Between measurements the amplitudes change smoothly and predictably, by rotating a vector, and amplitudes add before they are squared, so two routes to the same outcome can cancel each other. This is interference, and it is the source of everything that is distinctively quantum.

blocks.text: These sound abstract, and the first pages of the shelf (Why Quantum Mechanics: The Experiments (#/quantum/foundations/why-quantum)) show why anyone believes them: three experiments with magnets, polarising filters and single particles that no classical picture can explain. After that the shelf is calculation: you will compute probabilities, rotate qubits, find energy levels and describe systems of several qubits, and every result will be small enough to check by hand and on a computer.

Why learn it here? Because it is the language of quantum reservoir computing, the topic of the other shelf (Quantum Reservoir Computing (#/qrc)). A quantum reservoir is a register of interacting qubits that is driven by an input signal and read out to produce features for a simple learning step. To follow how it works you must be able to read a state vector, know what a measured average $\langle Z\rangle$ means and why it needs many repetitions, picture a qubit on the Bloch sphere, know that a Hamiltonian moves a state by $U = e^{-iHt}$, and work with tensor products, partial traces and density matrices. This shelf builds exactly those, in the notation the QRC pages use.
Who this shelf is for, and what you need first

It is for a capable adult who is learning on their own and wants to be able to do the calculations, not only to hear about them. You need to be comfortable with high-school algebra, with functions and graphs, and with the idea that a derivative is a rate of change. You do not need a physics course, a linear algebra course, complex numbers or any programming; the shelf teaches the mathematics it uses. The page Complex Numbers for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/complex-numbers) starts from $i^2 = -1$, and Linear Algebra for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/linear-algebra) starts from what a vector and a matrix are. You only need to be willing to work through steps on paper.

It is a working course, not a survey. Potential wells, the hydrogen atom and scattering are left out, not because they are unimportant but because QRC never uses them. What is in is finite-dimensional quantum mechanics (qubits and spins), plus one infinite-dimensional system, the harmonic oscillator, because continuous-variable reservoirs are built from it.
How long it takes

The shelf has 25 pages in four chapters: 8 in Foundations, 5 in Qubits, 5 in Dynamics and 7 in Many Qubits. A page is a few thousand words with worked examples and problems. Allowing about two hours a page if you do the exercises (an estimate, not a measurement) the whole shelf takes about 50 hours, which is two months at four or five hours a week. If you read without doing the problems, count on about half of that. You can stop early: the Path into QRC section below names the pages the QRC shelf cannot do without, and those are fewer than 25.
The four chapters and every page, in reading order
Read in this order, because each page assumes the ones before it.
Foundations: what a state, a measurement and an observable are
Foundations (#/quantum/foundations) teaches the mathematics and the first rules. States are vectors, measurement is probabilistic, and quantities you can measure are matrices with special properties.

items: Why Quantum Mechanics: The Experiments (#/quantum/foundations/why-quantum): Stern-Gerlach magnets, three polarisers and single particles in an interferometer, worked with numbers.
Complex Numbers for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/complex-numbers): the arithmetic of $i$, the complex plane, Euler's formula, and why adding amplitudes produces interference.
Linear Algebra for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/linear-algebra): inner products, Hermitian and unitary matrices, matrix exponentials and Kronecker products.
Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors): the directions a matrix only stretches, and the stretch factors.
States and Dirac Notation (#/quantum/foundations/states-and-dirac-notation): kets and bras, superposition, bases, and why global phase does not matter while relative phase does.
Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement): probabilities from amplitudes, collapse, measuring in other bases, and shot statistics.
Observables and Uncertainty (#/quantum/foundations/observables-and-uncertainty): expectation values, variance and the uncertainty relation.
Commutators and Compatible Observables (#/quantum/foundations/commutators): the commutator, compatible observables, and the generalised uncertainty relation derived.

blocks.text: Qubits: the two-level system and how to rotate it
Qubits (#/quantum/qubits) applies the rules to the smallest system, which is also the one a quantum computer is built from.

items: The Qubit and the Bloch Sphere (#/quantum/qubits/bloch-sphere): every pure qubit state as a point on a sphere whose coordinates are $\langle X\rangle$, $\langle Y\rangle$, $\langle Z\rangle$.
Pauli Operators and Rotations (#/quantum/qubits/pauli-and-rotations): the Pauli algebra and the rotations $e^{-i\theta P/2}$, including the rotation that writes an input into a qubit.
Interference of Amplitudes (#/quantum/qubits/interference): the Mach-Zehnder interferometer, which-path information, and how algorithms use interference.
Gates and Circuits (#/quantum/qubits/gates-and-circuits): Hadamard, CNOT, an $XX$ rotation from two CNOTs, and Trotter steps.
Driven Qubits and Rabi Oscillations (#/quantum/qubits/driven-qubits): precession in a field and how an oscillating drive makes a gate.

blocks.text: Dynamics: how states change in time
Dynamics (#/quantum/dynamics) adds time. A Hamiltonian generates motion, and conservation laws tell you what cannot change.

items: The Schrödinger Equation (#/quantum/dynamics/schrodinger-equation): $U = e^{-iHt}$, energy eigenstates, precession and Rabi oscillation.
Schrödinger and Heisenberg Pictures (#/quantum/dynamics/pictures-of-time-evolution): moving the state or moving the observables, with identical predictions.
Wavefunctions, Position and Momentum (#/quantum/dynamics/wavefunctions): a particle on a line, the continuous version of a qubit's two amplitudes.
Symmetries and Conservation (#/quantum/dynamics/symmetries-and-conservation): conserved quantities, parity and total $Z$, and splitting a Hamiltonian into blocks.
The Harmonic Oscillator (#/quantum/dynamics/harmonic-oscillator): evenly spaced levels from one commutator, coherent states, and the language of continuous-variable reservoirs.

blocks.text: Many Qubits: several systems, parts of systems and spin models
Many Qubits (#/quantum/many-body) is where the QRC shelf's objects first appear: interacting registers, entanglement, mixed states and the spin Hamiltonians of reservoirs.

items: Composite Systems and Tensor Products (#/quantum/many-body/composite-systems): Kronecker products, basis order and the $2^n$ growth.
Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement): Bell states, the Schmidt decomposition and entanglement entropy.
The Partial Trace and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/partial-trace): reduced states worked through step by step.
Bell Inequalities and Nonlocality (#/quantum/many-body/bell-inequalities): CHSH and the numbers $2$ and $2\sqrt2$.
Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states): the density matrix, purity and the Bloch ball.
Decoherence: How Superpositions Fade (#/quantum/many-body/decoherence): dephasing and amplitude damping from an environment.
Spin Models (#/quantum/many-body/spin-models): Ising, transverse-field Ising, XX and Heisenberg models, a phase transition and the disordered reservoir Hamiltonian.

blocks.text: The postulates in one place

All of the shelf rests on five rules. They are listed here so that you can come back to them; each one is explained in detail on the page named after it. Do not try to understand them all now. Read them once, and look back after the Foundations chapter.

items: States: a closed system is described by a unit vector $\vert\psi\rangle$ in a complex vector space (a Hilbert space). Vectors that differ only by an overall phase are the same state.
Observables: every measurable quantity is a Hermitian operator $A$; the possible results are its eigenvalues.

Measurement (the Born rule): measuring $A$ gives eigenvalue $a$ with probability $\Vert\Pi_a\vert\psi\rangle\Vert^2$, where $\Pi_a$ projects onto the eigenvectors with that eigenvalue, and leaves the state in $\Pi_a\vert\psi\rangle$, renormalised.

Dynamics: between measurements the state evolves by the Schrödinger equation $i\,\tfrac{d}{dt}\vert\psi\rangle = H\vert\psi\rangle$, so $\vert\psi(t)\rangle = e^{-iHt}\vert\psi(0)\rangle$ (units with $\hbar = 1$, as on every page here).
Composite systems: the state space of two systems is the tensor product of their spaces, so dimensions multiply.

blocks.text: What each postulate says, with a number

States. 'A unit vector' means the squares of the sizes of the amplitudes add to 1. The qubit state $\sqrt{0.8}\,\vert0\rangle + \sqrt{0.2}\,\vert1\rangle$ has $0.8 + 0.2 = 1$. Multiplying the whole vector by a phase $e^{i\gamma}$ changes no probability, because the size of $e^{i\gamma}\alpha$ equals the size of $\alpha$; that is why such vectors count as the same state. What does matter is the phase between amplitudes: $(\vert0\rangle + \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and $(\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ are different states (States and Dirac Notation (#/quantum/foundations/states-and-dirac-notation)).

Observables. The quantity 'spin along $x$' is represented by the matrix $X$ with rows $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$. It is Hermitian (equal to its conjugate transpose), which guarantees that its eigenvalues are real numbers, as measured quantities must be. Its eigenvalues are $+1$ and $-1$, with eigenvectors $\vert\pm\rangle = (\vert0\rangle\pm\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Those two numbers are the only results a measurement of $X$ can give (Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors)).

Measurement. For the state above and the observable $X$, the probability of $+1$ is $\vert\langle+\vert\psi\rangle\vert^2 = \tfrac12(\sqrt{0.8} + \sqrt{0.2})^2 = \tfrac12(1 + 2\sqrt{0.16}) = 0.9$, and of $-1$ is $0.1$. After you obtain $+1$ the state is $\vert+\rangle$, so measuring again gives $+1$ with certainty. The expectation value is $0.9(+1) + 0.1(-1) = 0.8$ (Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement)).

Dynamics. For a spin in a field along $z$ with Hamiltonian $H = \tfrac\omega2 Z$, the evolution leaves $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$ unchanged except for phases $e^{\mp i\omega t/2}$. Start in $\vert+\rangle$ and wait until $\omega t = \pi/2$: the relative phase has become $e^{i\pi/2} = i$, and the state is $(\vert0\rangle + i\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. The arrow on the Bloch sphere has rotated a quarter turn about $z$. The motion is reversible and nothing random happens until you measure (The Schrödinger Equation (#/quantum/dynamics/schrodinger-equation)).

Composite systems. Two qubits have the four amplitudes of $\vert00\rangle, \vert01\rangle, \vert10\rangle, \vert11\rangle$, not two plus two. Ten qubits have $2^{10} = 1024$ amplitudes and 50 qubits have $2^{50} = 1\,125\,899\,906\,842\,624$. Some states of two qubits cannot be split into one state for each: they are entangled (Composite Systems and Tensor Products (#/quantum/many-body/composite-systems) and Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement)).

Everything else, mixed states and channels included, follows from these five once you allow yourself to ignore part of a larger system. That last step is where the QRC shelf's Open Quantum Systems Toolkit (#/qrc/open-systems) picks up, and it begins in The Partial Trace and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/partial-trace) and Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states).
How to study this shelf

items: Do the Check yourself questions as you go. Each is a short question with a hint and a step-by-step solution at the end of a section. Cover the solution, try the question, and only then open it. If you cannot start, read the hint; if you still cannot, read the first step of the solution and try again from there. Getting one wrong and finding out why teaches more than reading three pages.

Do not skip the algebra. Worked examples are written as numbered steps with every intermediate result. Follow them with a pencil, and re-derive one or two without looking. The aim is that you could do the calculation on a new example.

Run the code. Almost every page has a Python sample that uses only numpy (and sometimes scipy). Install them with pip, copy the sample into a file, run it with python3, and compare the printed numbers with the ones quoted on the page. Then change one thing: a number, a state, a sign. Seeing a result move is how a formula becomes familiar. The samples are short on purpose; you can read all of each one.
Use the widgets. The interactive plots have a Try this paragraph that tells you what to set and what you should see; predict the outcome before you move the slider.

Keep the notation page open. The Variables and symbols section below lists every symbol, with all of its meanings; highlighting a symbol on any page shows them. Several letters have more than one meaning (for example $H$, $P$, $Q$, $S$), and the list says which is which.
Go back. Several pages build on a calculation from an earlier one, such as the Pauli products or the tensor-product rule. Returning to a page after you have used it is normal and productive.
Do not memorise the formulas. Learn what a formula says in words and how to derive it in a few lines; the page's Key points summarise those.

blocks.text: The path into QRC

The Quantum Reservoir Computing shelf (Quantum Reservoir Computing (#/qrc)) starts with classical reservoir computing in Reservoir Computing Foundations (#/qrc/foundations), which needs no quantum mechanics, so you can read it in parallel with this shelf. Its quantum chapters need the pages below.

items: Read the Foundations chapter in full except, if you are in a hurry, the commutators page. You need complex numbers, linear algebra, states, measurement and observables for everything.
Read the Qubits chapter up to and including gates and circuits. The driven-qubits and interference pages explain how real hardware and algorithms work; they are optional for the first pass.

From Dynamics, read the Schrödinger equation and the symmetries page. The pictures and wavefunctions pages are optional, and the harmonic oscillator is needed only for the continuous-variable reservoirs.
Read the Many Qubits chapter in order. It is the part most directly used: composite systems, entanglement, the partial trace, mixed states, decoherence and spin models.

Then go to Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels), which starts where Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states) and Decoherence: How Superpositions Fade (#/quantum/many-body/decoherence) end, and from there to The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir).

blocks.text: If you already know some quantum mechanics, the quickest check is the problems at the foot of each page: if they are easy, skip ahead.
Variables and symbols

The symbols used across this shelf. Some letters mean different things in different places; every meaning is listed, numbered, with the setting it belongs to. Every page sets $\hbar = 1$. Highlight a symbol on any page of the shelf to see its meanings.
States and amplitudes

items: $\vert\psi\rangle$: the state vector (ket) of the system; $\langle\psi\vert$ is its bra and $\vert\psi(t)\rangle$ the state at time $t$.

$\phi,\ \varphi$: (1) a second state, as in the inner product $\langle\phi\vert\psi\rangle$; (2) on the Bloch sphere: the azimuthal angle $\phi$ of a qubit state, $0\le\phi<2\pi$, which is the relative phase between $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$; (3) a phase or rotation angle, as in $\vert0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\vert1\rangle$ or $R_Z(\varphi)$.

$\alpha$: (1) the amplitude of $\vert0\rangle$ in a qubit state $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$, with $\vert\alpha\vert^2 + \vert\beta\vert^2 = 1$; (2) for an oscillator: the complex amplitude of a coherent state $\vert\alpha\rangle$, the eigenvalue in $a\vert\alpha\rangle = \alpha\vert\alpha\rangle$; $\vert\alpha\vert^2$ is the mean photon number.
$\beta$: the amplitude of $\vert1\rangle$ in a qubit state $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$.

$\theta$: (1) on the Bloch sphere: the polar angle of a qubit state, $\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\vert0\rangle + e^{i\phi}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\vert1\rangle$, so $P(1) = \sin^2(\theta/2)$; (2) the angle of a rotation gate, $R_P(\theta) = e^{-i\theta P/2}$; (3) an angle that sets a two-qubit state, as in $\cos\theta\vert00\rangle + \sin\theta\vert11\rangle$.
$\gamma$: a global phase: $e^{i\gamma}\vert\psi\rangle$ is the same physical state as $\vert\psi\rangle$.
$c_k$: the amplitude of a basis state in an expansion, most often $c_k = \langle E_k\vert\psi(0)\rangle$ for energy eigenstate $\vert E_k\rangle$, which then evolves as $c_k e^{-iE_kt}$.
$\vert e_k\rangle$: the vectors of an orthonormal measurement basis; outcome $k$ has probability $\vert\langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle\vert^2$.
$s$: the input value $s\in[0,1]$ written into a qubit as $\vert\psi_s\rangle = \sqrt{1-s}\,\vert0\rangle + \sqrt{s}\,\vert1\rangle$, the encoding the QRC shelf uses.
$d$: the dimension of a Hilbert space (the number of levels); $d = 2^n$ for $n$ qubits.

$n,\ \hat n$: (1) the number of qubits; $n$ qubits need $2^n$ amplitudes; (2) for an oscillator: the number of quanta in the Fock state $\vert n\rangle$, the eigenvalue of $a^\dagger a$; (3) $\hat n$: a unit vector giving a rotation axis, as in $e^{-i\theta\,\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$.

$\vec r,\ r$: (1) $\vec r$: the Bloch vector $(\langle X\rangle, \langle Y\rangle, \langle Z\rangle)$; $\vert\vec r\vert = 1$ for a pure state and less for a mixed one; (2) the number of Trotter steps a time evolution is split into; the first-order error falls as $t^2/r$.
$\rho,\ \rho_A$: the density matrix, $\rho = \sum_j p_j\vert\psi_j\rangle\langle\psi_j\vert$; $\rho_A = \operatorname{Tr}_B\rho$ and $\rho_B$ are the reduced density matrices of the two parts.

$p,\ p_j$: (1) a probability: of preparing $\vert\psi_j\rangle$ in a mixture ($p_j$) or of measurement outcome $k$ ($p_k = \operatorname{Tr}(\Pi_k\rho)$); (2) for an oscillator: the momentum quadrature $p = i(a^\dagger - a)/\sqrt2$, with $[x, p] = i$.
$x$: for an oscillator: the position quadrature $x = (a + a^\dagger)/\sqrt2$.
$\vert0\rangle$, $\vert1\rangle$, $\vert\pm\rangle$: the computational basis and the $X$ eigenstates $(\vert0\rangle\pm\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
$\vert\Phi^\pm\rangle$, $\vert\Psi^\pm\rangle$: the four Bell states.

blocks.text: Operators and gates

items: $H,\ H_d$: (1) the Hamiltonian, the energy observable that generates time evolution, $\vert\psi(t)\rangle = e^{-iHt}\vert\psi(0)\rangle$; (2) $H_d$: the Hadamard gate, written with a subscript so it is not confused with the Hamiltonian.
$U$: a unitary matrix, usually the time-evolution operator $U(t) = e^{-iHt}$.
$I$: the identity matrix (or operator); $I/d$ is the maximally mixed state.
$i$: the imaginary unit, $i^2 = -1$; as a subscript, $i$ labels a qubit (as in $Z_i$).
$X,\ X_i$: the Pauli $X$ matrix, a bit flip; $X_i$ is $X$ acting on qubit $i$.
$Y,\ Y_i$: the Pauli $Y$ matrix; $Y_i$ is $Y$ acting on qubit $i$.
$Z,\ Z_i$: the Pauli $Z$ matrix, diagonal in the computational basis; $Z_i$ acts on qubit $i$ and $\langle Z_i\rangle$ is the usual reservoir feature.

$\sigma,\ \vec\sigma$: (1) $\vec\sigma = (X, Y, Z)$: the vector of Pauli matrices, so $\rho = \tfrac12(I + \vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)$; $\sigma^\pm$ are the raising and lowering operators; (2) a standard deviation: $\sigma_A$ is the spread of observable $A$'s outcomes, as in $\sigma_A\sigma_B \ge \tfrac12\vert\langle[A,B]\rangle\vert$, and $\sigma(\hat z)$ the shot-noise spread of an estimate.
$R_X,\ R_Y,\ R_Z,\ R_P$: rotation gates: $R_P(\theta) = e^{-i\theta P/2}$ turns the Bloch vector by $\theta$ about the $P$ axis.

$P,\ Q$: (1) a generic Pauli operator, as in $R_P(\theta)$ or $\operatorname{Tr}(PQ) = 2\delta_{PQ}$; (2) a probability: $P(0)$, $P(1)$ of a measurement outcome, or $P_1(t)$ of finding the qubit in $\vert1\rangle$ at time $t$.
$Q$: (1) a conserved quantity: an operator with $[H, Q] = 0$, whose eigenspaces the evolution never mixes; (2) a second generic Pauli operator, as in $P_iQ_j$.

$S$: (1) the phase gate $S = \mathrm{diag}(1, i)$; (2) the number of shots (repetitions) used to estimate an expectation value; the error falls as $1/\sqrt{S}$; (3) the entanglement entropy $S = -\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A\log_2\rho_A$.

$\Pi$: (1) $\Pi_a$: the projector onto the eigenspace of eigenvalue $a$; outcome $a$ has probability $\Vert\Pi_a\vert\psi\rangle\Vert^2$; (2) the parity operator $\Pi = Z_1Z_2\cdots Z_n$, conserved by Hamiltonians built from $X_iX_j$ and $Z_i$.
$a,\ a^\dagger$: (1) for an oscillator: the annihilation operator $a$, which removes one quantum; $a^\dagger$ is the creation operator; (2) an eigenvalue label, as in $A = \sum_a a\,\Pi_a$.
$A,\ B$: (1) a generic observable or matrix; $A^\dagger$ is its adjoint; (2) the first part of a composite system, as in $\rho_A$ and $\vert\psi\rangle_{AB}$.
$B$: (1) a second generic observable or matrix; (2) the second part of a composite system, as in $\rho_A = \operatorname{Tr}_B\rho$.
$E_k,\ \vert E_k\rangle$: the energy eigenvalues and eigenstates of $H$; $E_0$ is the ground-state energy.

$\lambda_k$: (1) the eigenvalues of a matrix, as in $A = \sum_k\lambda_k v_kv_k^\dagger$; (2) the Schmidt coefficients, $\vert\psi\rangle_{AB} = \sum_k\lambda_k\vert a_k\rangle\otimes\vert b_k\rangle$.
$v_k$: the eigenvectors in a spectral decomposition; $V$ is the unitary whose columns they are.
$V$: (1) the matrix of eigenvectors in $A = V\,\mathrm{diag}(\lambda)\,V^\dagger$; (2) in QRC: the number of virtual nodes, the times the reservoir is read between two inputs.
$k$: a running index: a basis vector, an eigenvalue, or the input step in QRC.

blocks.text: Dynamics and spin models

items: $t$: time.
$\Delta t$: the time a reservoir evolves between inputs, $U = e^{-iH\Delta t}$.
$\Omega$: the Rabi frequency, the strength of a drive, in $H = \tfrac\delta2 Z + \tfrac\Omega2 X$.
$\delta$: (1) the detuning of a drive from resonance, in $H = \tfrac\delta2 Z + \tfrac\Omega2 X$; (2) $\delta_{PQ}$: the Kronecker delta, 1 when $P = Q$ and 0 otherwise.
$h,\ h_i$: the field on each spin, the $h_iZ_i$ terms of a spin Hamiltonian ($h$ when it is the same on every spin).
$g_i$: a field along $x$, the $g_iX_i$ terms of a spin Hamiltonian.
$J,\ J_{ij}$: the coupling strength between spins $i$ and $j$ ($J$ when it is uniform).
$\hbar$: the reduced Planck constant; every page sets $\hbar = 1$.

blocks.text: Units: every page sets $\hbar = 1$, so energies and frequencies are measured in the same units and $e^{-iHt}$ needs no constant. Qubit convention: $\vert0\rangle$ has $Z = +1$ and $\vert1\rangle$ has $Z = -1$, and in a register the leftmost tensor factor is qubit 1, exactly as on the QRC pages.
